To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV infection and antiretrovirals have widespread effects on the immune system, including the ability of the immune system to control mycobacterial infection and prevent disease.
HIV infection and ART exert widespread effects on the immune response to mycobacteria, and that the TST is a powerful tool for studying these effects in vivo.
HIV-1 infection and ART exert widespread changes to human immunity at the tissue level, which can impair the optimal host protective immune response to TB.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular dissection of the effects of HIV-1 on human immunity in active tuberculosis.
understanding the mechanisms by which HIV-1 and ART alter the immune response to Mycobacterium Tuberculosis.
the molecular mechanisms of host immunity and susceptibility to tuberculosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV-1 infection and antiretro-viral therapy (ART), in the presence of Mycobacterium TB, result in a dysregulated immune response, with an imbalance in the Th1/Th2 responses.

the molecular dissection of HIV-1/Tuberculosis (TB) co-infection has revealed novel mechanisms by which HIV-1 infection impairs the optimal host protective immune response against TB and provides a framework for host-directed therapies to improve outcomes in this setting.
the effects of HIV on immune responses to TB in active disease are complex and multifaceted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

HIV-1 infection causes widespread dysregulation of immune responses to M. tuberculosis infection in the tissue microenvironment, and that this may be a key mechanism for increased susceptibility to TB disease.

HIV-1 infection in active TB patients results in a spectrum of immunopathologies that can be detected in the skin and that are associated with increased risk for TB disease, but that these effects are localised to the skin, not evident systemically, and are potentially treatable.

HIV-1 infection causes profound dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses in human TB, which is not limited to CD4 T cells but also extends to other arms of the immune system, and is associated with increased risk and pathogenesis of disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV-1 infection and ART have profound, but distinct, effects on immune responses to M tuberculosis.
HIV-1 infection has a profound and complex impact on the immune system, which is only partly reversed by ART.

HIV-1 infection and ART have profound and widespread effects on human immunity, including the tissue microenvironment, and that these effects are not uniform across the immune system and are associated with differential risk of TB.
